skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. //==================================================================================================
5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================
7. 
8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("number.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("number.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use crate::mem;
15. 
16. //==================================================================================================
17. // Structures
18. //==================================================================================================
19. 
20. ///
21. /// # Description
22. ///
23. /// A type that represents a frame number.
24. /// A frame number is in the range from `0` to [`Self::MAX`] (inclusive).
25. ///
26. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
27. pub struct FrameNumber(usize);
28. 
29. //==================================================================================================
30. // Implementations
31. //==================================================================================================
32. 
33. impl FrameNumber {
34.     /// The maximum frame number.
35.     pub const MAX: usize = mem::MAX_ADDRESS / mem::FRAME_SIZE - 1;
36. 
37.     pub const NULL: Self = Self(0);
38. 
39.     ///
40.     /// # Description
41.     ///
42.     /// Constructs a [`FrameNumber`].
43.     ///
44.     /// # Parameters
45.     ///
46.     /// - `value`: The value of the frame number.
47.     ///
48.     /// # Returns
49.     ///
50.     /// - `Some(`[`FrameNumber`]`)`: Upon success.
51.     /// - `None`: If the value is greater than [`Self::MAX`].
52.     ///
53.     pub fn from_raw_value(value: usize) -> Option<Self> {
54.         if value > Self::MAX {
55.             return None;
56.         }
57. 
58.         Some(Self(value))
59.     }
60. 
61.     ///
62.     /// # Description
63.     ///
64.     /// Converts a [`FrameNumber`] into a raw value.
65.     ///
66.     /// # Returns
67.     ///
68.     /// The raw value of the target [`FrameNumber`].
69.     ///
70.     pub fn into_raw_value(self) -> usize {
71.         self.0
72.     }
73. }
74. 
75. //==================================================================================================
76. // Unit Tests
77. //==================================================================================================
78. 
79. /// Tests if [`FrameNumber::from_raw_value()`] successfully constructs frame zero.
80. #[test]
81. fn test_frame_number_from_raw_value_zero() {
82.     let raw_value: usize = 0;
83.     let frame_number: FrameNumber = FrameNumber::from_raw_value(raw_value).unwrap();
84.     assert_eq!(frame_number.into_raw_value(), raw_value);
85. }
86. 
87. /// Tests if [`FrameNumber::from_raw_value()`] successfully constructs the maximum frame number.
88. #[test]
89. fn test_frame_number_from_raw_value_max() {
90.     let raw_value: usize = FrameNumber::MAX;
91.     let frame_number: FrameNumber = FrameNumber::from_raw_value(raw_value).unwrap();
92.     assert_eq!(frame_number.into_raw_value(), raw_value);
93. }
94.

1. # View Design: `FrameNumber` (`arch/src/x86/mem/paging/frame/number.rs`)
2. 
3. > Scope: design the abstract `View` (+ `inv`) for `FrameNumber` that the
4. > in-scope verification-order targets will reference in later spec/proof phases.
5. >
6. > In-scope targets: the type `FrameNumber` (its `View` and `inv`),
7. > `FrameNumber::from_raw_value`, `FrameNumber::into_raw_value`.
8. > Out of scope and untouched: nothing else lives in this module — only the two
9. > `#[test]` functions, which are de-facto callers, not targets.
10. >
11. > Unlike the sibling `FrameAddress`, **no `View`/`inv` skeleton exists yet**:
12. > `number.rs` carries no `#[verus_spec]`, and `number.spec.rs` /
13. > `number.proof.rs` are empty `verus! { }` blocks. This is therefore a *fresh*
14. > design rather than a confirmation. It is also a **real, in-module**
15. > verification target (its bodies will be verified — it is **not**
16. > `external_body`/trusted). The boundary contracts recorded for `FrameNumber`
17. > in `verus-ai-logs/tcb-allowed.md` are the *callers'* trust assumptions stated
18. > in `phys.spec.rs`; this View is the in-module abstraction those assumptions
19. > must agree with.
20. 
21. ---
22. 
23. ## Abstract Resource
24. 
25. `FrameNumber` is, to its callers, **the abstract identity of one physical page
26. frame**: a bounded non-negative integer index in `0 ..= MAX` (where
27. `MAX = MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE − 1`). It is a `Copy` value object — not an
28. owning resource, collection, or state machine — whose only observable state is
29. a single mathematical integer: the raw frame index.
30. 
31. It is the validated currency three subsystems exchange:
32. 
33. - the **physical-frame allocator / refcount layer** (`mm::phys::frame.rs`),
34.   which produces a raw allocator index, validates it through `from_raw_value`,
35.   and later uses `into_raw_value` as an index into its `refcount` array;
36. - the **hardware paging layer** (`pde.rs`, `pte.rs`, `page_table.rs`,
37.   `page_directory.rs`), which decodes a frame field out of a page-table word
38.   (`>> FRAME_SHIFT` → `from_raw_value`) and re-encodes it
39.   (`into_raw_value` → `<< FRAME_SHIFT`); and
40. - the **address tower** (`PhysicalAddress::into_frame_number` /
41.   `from_number` in `phys.rs`), which converts between a frame index and a
42.   physical address (`index * FRAME_SIZE`).
43. 
44. Callers reason about a `FrameNumber` through exactly **two equivalent identities
45. of the same underlying integer**:
46. 
47. - the **raw frame index** — `from_raw_value` (validate `usize → Option<Self>`)
48.   and `into_raw_value` (project `Self → usize`); and
49. - the **sentinel** `NULL` (= frame `0`) and the **inclusive bound** `MAX`.
50. 
51. That it is internally a `usize` newtype is invisible to callers: the analysis is
52. explicit that callers "don't care about the internal representation (a `usize`
53. newtype) — only the round-trip and the range boundary matter."
54. 
55. ---
56. 
57. ## View Struct
58. 
59. The abstract state of a `FrameNumber` is **exactly one value**: the raw frame
60. index as an unbounded integer. Verus models this with a **scalar `View`
61. (`type V = int`)**, not a one-field record struct, because there is only one
62. caller-observable quantity. This matches the rest of the address/frame family
63. (`PhysicalAddress@ : int`, `VirtualAddress@ : int`, `PageAligned<T>@ : int`,
64. `FrameAddress@ : int`), confirming the abstraction is caller-driven, not
65. implementation-driven.
66. 
67. ```rust
68. impl View for FrameNumber {
69.     type V = int;
70. 
71.     // `closed`: callers may reference `self@` (the abstract frame index as an
72.     // unbounded integer), but the newtype mapping `self.0 as int` is hidden.
73.     // The abstract value is "the index of the physical frame this handle names".
74.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
75.         self.0 as int   // newtype identity: the inner usize, lifted to int
76.     }
77. }
78. ```
79. 
80. `self@ : int` is the entire abstract state. `view()` is **`closed`** so the
81. `usize`-newtype mapping does not leak; callers still obtain a usable `int`
82. (`f@`) for indexing, the `index * FRAME_SIZE` / `index << FRAME_SHIFT`
83. arithmetic their no-overflow proofs need, comparison, and equality. The
84. round-trip back to a concrete `usize` is supplied by the `into_raw_value`
85. contract (`result as int == self@`), not by exposing the mapping.
86. 
87. ### Equivalent "single-field" reading
88. 
89. ```rust
90. pub struct FrameNumberView {
91.     // index: the index of the physical frame this handle names, as `int`.
92.     //        The only state a caller can observe. "In range `0 ..= MAX`" is a
93.     //        *property* of this value (captured by `inv`), not a separate field;
94.     //        the corresponding physical address (`index * FRAME_SIZE`) and PTE
95.     //        field (`index << FRAME_SHIFT`) are *derived projections*, not state.
96.     index: int,
97. }
98. ```
99.

166. and the `FrameNumber` that denotes it. These are expressed directly with the

176.   constructor.

217. rewritten with a different algorithm, would this field still make sense?"*:

220. |-------|-------------------|---------|

236.   agrees with equality of `self@`; no field.

274.    `index * FRAME_SIZE`).**

276.    `FrameNumber`. The heaviest-used callers (`refcount` indexing in

278.    `from_raw_value` is handed a raw index. Making the View the address would
279.    force a `/ FRAME_SIZE` in nearly every contract and lose the direct

288.    shift is a derived projection of `self@`, not state.

309.    `result as int == self@` bridge) without depending on the inner `usize`
310.    representation.

    the `into_raw_value` contract (`result as int == self@`).

    `FrameNumber`. The heaviest-used callers (`refcount` indexing in

    force a `/ FRAME_SIZE` in nearly every contract and lose the direct

    more fundamental, lower-friction abstraction here; the address is recovered by
    multiplication (and is `FrameAddress`'s job).

    shift is a derived projection of `self@`, not state.

    load-bearing well-formedness fact — without it, callers' no-overflow proofs
    for `index << FRAME_SHIFT` and `index * FRAME_SIZE` cannot be discharged, and

    is safe to require because `from_raw_value` (the only public constructor) and
    `NULL` both establish it.
 
 6. **Naming the bound differently from the callers' `spec_max_frame_number()`
    (e.g. a fresh `spec_frame_number_max()`).**
    Rejected: the upstream callers' assumed contracts in `phys.spec.rs` /
    `tcb-allowed.md` are already stated against `spec_max_frame_number()`. Reusing
    that exact name makes the in-module real contract and the assumed contract
    definitionally identical, so verifying this module directly discharges the
    assumption the callers trusted — no bridging lemma needed.
 
 7. **Open `view()` (exposing `self.0 as int`).**
    Rejected: the skill mandates `view()` be `closed` so the newtype mapping does
    not leak; callers get all they need (`f@`, plus `into_raw_value`'s

1. ---
2. name: verus-constraints
3. description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Verus Constraints
7. 
8. ## Attribute Style for Exec Functions
9. 
10. All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
11. (`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
12. See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.
13. 
14. ```rust
15. // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
16. #[verus_spec(ret =>
17.     requires x < 100,
18.     ensures ret == x + 1,
19. )]
20. fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
21.     x + 1
22. }
23. 
24. // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
25. verus! {
26.     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
27.         requires x < 100,
28.         ensures ret == x + 1,
29.     { x + 1 }
30. } // verus!
31. ```
32. 
33. **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
34. - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
35. - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
36. 
37. Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
38. signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.
39. 
40. ## Source Integrity (exec code)
41. 
42. The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
43. `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
44. 
45. Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
46. exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
47. constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
48. minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
49. 
50. **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
51. comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
52. 
53. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):
54. 
55. 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
56. 2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
57.    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
58. 3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
59.    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
60.    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
61.    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
62.    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
63.    the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
64.    `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.
65. 
66. **The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
67. There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
68. verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
69. rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.
70. 
71. **Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
72. `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
73. constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
74. copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.
75. 
76. - **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
77. - **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
78.   derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
79.   the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
80.   `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
81.   duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
82.   in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
83. - **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
84.   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
85.   `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
86.   `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.
87. 
88. **Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
89. `proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
90. on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
91. vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
92. used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
93. `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
94. state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
95. `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.
96. 
97. **After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
98. source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.
99. 
100. ## Forbidden Patterns
101. 
102. | Pattern | Policy |
103. |---|---|
104. | `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
105. | `assume(...)` | Banned |
106. | `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
107. | `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
108. | `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
109. | `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
110. | `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
111. | `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
112. | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
113. | `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |
114.

116.

 ```rust
 // ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
 #[verus_spec(ret =>
     requires x < 100,
     ensures ret == x + 1,
 )]
 fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
     x + 1
 }
 
 // ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
 verus! {
     fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
         requires x < 100,
         ensures ret == x + 1,
     { x + 1 }
 } // verus!
 ```
 
 **`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
 - `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
 - Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)
 
 Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
 signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

 The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
 `*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.
 
 Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
 exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
 constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
 minimal so developers can review diffs easily.
 
 **Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
 comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.
 
 The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):
 
 1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
 2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
    vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
 3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
    strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
    functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
    (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
    record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
    the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
    `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

 There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
 verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
 rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

 `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or

   duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**

   cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add

1. ---
2. name: spec-design
3. description: "How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Spec Design Guide
7. 
8. ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
9. 
10. ### Qualities of a Good Spec
11. 
12. 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
13.    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
14.    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
15. 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
16.    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
17.    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
18.    verifies the copy, not the real code.
19. 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
20.    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
21.    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
22. 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
23.    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
24.    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
25. 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
26.    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
27.    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
28.    recursive spec functions.
29. 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
30.    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
31.    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
32.    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
33.    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
34. 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
35.    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
36.    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
37.    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
38.    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
39. 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
40.    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
41.    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
42.    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
43.    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
44.    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
45.    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
46.    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
47.    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
48.    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
49.    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
50. 
51. ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
52. 
53. If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
54. nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
55. spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
56. design model.
57. 
58. 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
59.    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
60.    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
61.    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
62.    annotation beats no annotation.
63. 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
64.    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
65.    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
66.    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
67.    Always search vstd first.
68. 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
69.    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
70.    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
71.    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
72.    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
73.    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
74.    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
75.    by vstd.
76.    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
77.    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
78.    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
79.    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
80. 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
81.    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
82. 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
83.    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
84.    make Verus pass.
85.    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
86.    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
87.    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.
88. 
89. ### Anti-Patterns (reject or remove)
90. 
91. 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
92.    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
93.    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
94.    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
95.    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
96.    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
97.    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
98.    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
99.    
100.    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
101.    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.
102. 2. **Verification Escape** — using `assume`, `admit`,
103.    or `exec_allows_no_decreases_clause` to bypass verification. Fix the
104.    spec or proof instead.
105.    
106.    **Exceptions (legitimate trust boundaries):**
107.    - `assume_specification`: for std library / external functions whose
108.      source code is outside the verification scope (e.g., not in our
109.      crate). Write the spec to match the original API documentation.
110. 
111.    **assume_specification Audit Checklist:**
112. 
113.    1. **Read the official docs first**: find the function's doc comments

 # Spec Design Guide
 
 ## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles
 
 ### Qualities of a Good Spec
 
 1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
    `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
    functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
 2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
    exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
    copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
    verifies the copy, not the real code.
 3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
    that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
    that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
 4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
    not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
    bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
 5. **Simpler than the code** — the spec should be at a higher level of
    abstraction than the implementation. For example, where the code has
    loops, the spec may use `forall`, `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` operations, or
    recursive spec functions.
 6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
    If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
    test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
    type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
    If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
 7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
    over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
    `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
    addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
    non-negative and bounded by the address space.
 8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
    writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
    this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
    unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
    directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
    (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
    `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
    vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
    implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
    and return values through the module's public spec interface,
    `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.
 
 ### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria
 
 If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
 nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
 spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
 design model.
 
 1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
    by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
    module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
    and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
    annotation beats no annotation.
 2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
    provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
    `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
    functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
    Always search vstd first.
 3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
    module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
    `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
    specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
    annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`
    for project-internal code (any crate in the workspace). `assume_specification`
    is only for third-party dependencies and std library functions not covered
    by vstd.
    **Why this works without `admit()`**: `--verify-module M` only verifies
    functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
    trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
    verified later, the specs become fully proven.
 5. **No floating specs** — every spec function and lemma must ultimately
    connect to an exec contract. Orphan specs are dead code.
 6. **No `external_body` on current module** — the current module's functions
    must never be marked `external_body`. Use `admit()` in proof bodies to
    make Verus pass.
    **Dependency functions** in other modules may be marked `external_body`
    with `requires`/`ensures` to provide contracts that the current module
    can rely on. These are removed when the dependency module is verified.

 1. **Exec Code Mutation** — modifying existing exec code, APIs, or
    struct definitions to accommodate specs. Do not change function
    signatures, alter control flow, or add exec fields to structs.
    Adding `Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` fields is allowed — they are
    erased at compile time and do not change exec behavior. However,
    prefer keeping ghost state in spec.rs (e.g., on the View type)
    rather than adding fields to exec structs; only add when the proof
    genuinely requires ghost state to flow through exec code.
    
    Exec code must NOT be changed — the code has been pre-refactored to be
    fully Verus-compatible. See `verus-constraints` skill.

42. // ── Frame-number trust-boundary projections (arch `FrameNumber`) ──────────────
43. //
44. // `FrameNumber` lives in the `arch` crate, which is not Verus-enabled and has no
45. // `View` impl reachable here (orphan rule). Its abstract index is therefore
46. // projected by an uninterpreted ghost function, exactly as `view_design.md`
47. // prescribes. `spec_max_frame_number()` denotes `FrameNumber::MAX`.
48. 
49. // The integer index of a frame number (`0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()`).
50. pub uninterp spec fn spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int;
51. 
52. // The largest representable frame number. Mirrors `arch FrameNumber::MAX ==
53. // MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1 == usize::MAX / FRAME_SIZE - 1`. Interpreting it
54. // against `usize::MAX` and `spec_page_size()` is what lets verified constructors
55. // discharge their `usize` multiply (no-overflow) obligation: a frame index in
56. // `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()` scaled by `spec_page_size()` stays `<= usize::MAX`.
57. pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
58.     usize::MAX as int / spec_page_size() - 1
59. }
60. 
61. // ── Derived spec helpers over the View domain (`int`) ─────────────────────────
62. 
63. // The frame an address lies in: exact integer division, independent of whether
64. // the implementation shifts (`>> FRAME_SHIFT`) or divides (`/ FRAME_SIZE`).
65. pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
66.     addr_view / spec_page_size()
67. }
68. 
69. // The base (frame-aligned) address of a frame index: `frame * FRAME_SIZE`.
70. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
71.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
72. }
73. 
74. // ── `arch`/`sys` library-edge `assume_specification`s ─────────────────────────
75. 
76. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE` is the frame size (alias of `PAGE_SIZE`), tied to the
77. // canonical `spec_page_size()`. It is strictly positive (`== 4096`); positivity is
78. // the load-bearing fact for the division/modulo reasoning in the constructors.
79. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SIZE ] -> (result: usize)
80.     ensures
81.         result == spec_page_size(),
82.         spec_page_size() > 0,
83. ;
84. 
85. // `::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT == log2(FRAME_SIZE)`. Bounded below the pointer width
86. // so `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` is well-defined, and `2^FRAME_SHIFT == FRAME_SIZE`
87. // so the shift coincides with division by `spec_page_size()`.
88. pub assume_specification[ ::arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT ] -> (result: usize)
89.     ensures
90.         result < usize::BITS,
91.         pow2(result as nat) == spec_page_size(),
92. ;
93.

95. // (`mm::address::virt`), so its contract is imported directly across the crate
96. // boundary; a local `assume_specification` here would duplicate it (Verus error:
97. // "duplicate specification for ... ::new"). The guaranteed fact is identical
98. // (`result@ == value as int`).
99. 
100. // `<VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value` is pure newtype identity: the
101. // returned raw `usize` equals the abstract address. It remains an
102. // `assume_specification` trust boundary because this trait-impl method cannot be
103. // body-verified in `sys` without marking the whole `impl Address for
104. // VirtualAddress` verified, which pulls the sibling `as_ptr`/`as_mut_ptr` methods
105. // (unsupported `usize as *const u8` casts) into scope — a Verus front-end
106. // limitation (see `verus-ai-logs/verus-unsupported.md`).
107. pub assume_specification[ <VirtualAddress as Address>::into_raw_value ](
108.     addr: VirtualAddress,
109. ) -> (result: usize)
110.     ensures
111.         result as int == addr@,
112. ;
113. 
114. // `FrameNumber::into_raw_value` projects a frame number to its index; every
115. // `FrameNumber` value is in range (`0 ..= MAX`) by construction.
116. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::into_raw_value ](frame: FrameNumber) -> (result: usize)
117.     ensures
118.         result as int == spec_frame_raw_value(frame),
119.         0 <= spec_frame_raw_value(frame) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
120. ;
121. 
122. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` succeeds iff `value <= MAX`, preserving the index.
123. pub assume_specification[ FrameNumber::from_raw_value ](value: usize) -> (result: Option<FrameNumber>)
124.     ensures
125.         match result {
126.             Some(f) => value as int <= spec_max_frame_number()
127.                 && spec_frame_raw_value(f) == value as int,
128.             None => value as int > spec_max_frame_number(),
129.         },
130. ;
131. 
132. // ── Type invariant ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
133. //
134. // Every `PhysicalAddress` a verified constructor produces has a *representable
135. // frame number*: `self@ / FRAME_SIZE <= FrameNumber::MAX`. This is the load-
136. // bearing fact that makes `into_frame_number` total (its internal
137. // `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never panics), which the frame
138. // allocator relies on when using the result directly as a bitmap / refcount
139. // index. It is *not* alignment (MMIO addresses may be unaligned) and *not*
140. // RAM-validity (`from_mmio_address` deliberately bypasses that check).
141. impl PhysicalAddress {
142.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
143.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
144.     }

78. // representation.

data.deltaContent: I
'm verifying arch with no features enabled through cargo, and
the rustc-dep-of-std flag for arch only gets activated transitively when sysalloc or syscall are
built in that configuration—which is separate from the standard build.
Now I'm considering whether making vstd a hard dependency would cause issues when those components
build arch with rustc-dep-of-std enabled.
Looking
at how bitmap and bump-allocator handle this—they both have vstd as a hard dependency with unconditional imports,
and they compile fine in normal mode since vstd's ghost code gets erased. The real
question is whether the rustc-dep-of-std path for arch (through sysalloc/syscall) would break,
but that's only relevant if `make build` actually exercises that path for
the user-space libc build. Since the constraint requires the vstd import to remain
unconditional and not cfg-gated, vstd has to be available during normal cargo builds anyway, so it can't be optional.
I
'll just make the change and test it—adding vstd as
a dependency to arch's Cargo.toml and including the metadata.verus configuration,
then running `make build` to see if it works.

+verus! {
+
+use crate::mem;
+
+// ── Frame size / representability bound ───────────────────────────────────────
+//
+// `FrameNumber` is, to its callers, the abstract identity of one physical page
+// frame: a bounded non-negative integer index. The two spec constants below fix
+// the vocabulary every contract speaks. They share the names the upstream
+// callers already trust in `phys.spec.rs` / `tcb-allowed.md`, so the in-module
+// contracts and the callers' assumed contracts coincide by construction.
+
+// The frame size as an unbounded integer, tied to the exec `mem::FRAME_SIZE`
+// (an alias of `PAGE_SIZE`). Strictly positive; positivity is the load-bearing
+// fact behind the no-overflow reasoning of every caller that scales a frame
+// index by the frame size.
+pub open spec fn spec_frame_size() -> int {
+    mem::FRAME_SIZE as int
+}
+
+// The inclusive maximum frame index, mirroring the exec
+// `FrameNumber::MAX == mem::MAX_ADDRESS / mem::FRAME_SIZE - 1`. A frame index in
+// `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()` scaled by `spec_frame_size()` stays within
+// `usize`, which is exactly the no-overflow guarantee `phys.rs::from_number`,
+// `pde.rs` and `pte.rs` depend on.
+pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
+    mem::MAX_ADDRESS as int / spec_frame_size() - 1
+}
+
+// ── View ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
+//
+// A `FrameNumber` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the raw frame
+// index. `closed` so the `usize`-newtype mapping does not leak; callers still
+// obtain a usable `int` (`f@`) for indexing, arithmetic and comparison, while
+// the concrete `usize` is recovered through `into_raw_value`'s contract
+// (`result as int == self@`).
+impl View for FrameNumber {
+    type V = int;
+
+    closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
+        self.0 as int
+    }
+}
+
+// ── Well-formedness invariant ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
+//
+// Every `FrameNumber` names a representable frame: its index lies in
+// `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()`. Declared as a `#[verifier::type_invariant]`
+// so the bound holds for *every* value of the type without a precondition —
+// `into_raw_value`'s callers rely on the range unconditionally (they never hold
+// a precondition obligation when projecting a frame they already own). Stated
+// purely over the abstract index `self@`, independent of the inner `usize`.
+impl FrameNumber {
+    #[verifier::type_invariant]
+    pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
+        &&& 0 <= self@
+        &&& self@ <= spec_max_frame_number()
+    }
+}
+
+} // verus!

+// `usize`, which is exactly the no-overflow guarantee `phys.rs::from_number`,
+// `pde.rs` and `pte.rs` depend on.
+pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
+    mem::MAX_ADDRESS as int / spec_frame_size() - 1
+}
+
+// ── View ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
+//
+// A `FrameNumber` abstracts to a single mathematical integer: the raw frame
+// index. `closed` so the `usize`-newtype mapping does not leak; callers still
+// obtain a usable `int` (`f@`) for indexing, arithmetic and comparison, while
+// the concrete `usize` is recovered through `into_raw_value`'s contract
+// (`result as int == self@`).
+impl View for FrameNumber {
+    type V = int;
+
+    closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
+        self.0 as int
+    }
+}
+
+// ── Well-formedness invariant ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
+//
+// Every `FrameNumber` names a representable frame: its index lies in
+// `0 ..= spec_max_frame_number()`. Declared as a `#[verifier::type_invariant]`
+// so the bound holds for *every* value of the type without a precondition —
+// `into_raw_value`'s callers rely on the range unconditionally (they never hold
+// a precondition obligation when projecting a frame they already own). Stated
+// purely over the abstract index `self@`, independent of the inner `usize`.
+impl FrameNumber {
+    #[verifier::type_invariant]
+    pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
+        &&& 0 <= self@
+        &&& self@ <= spec_max_frame_number()
+    }
+}
+
+} // verus!
